For those preferring traditional domestic arrangements, we direct your attention to the growing availability of certified live-in professionals.

The man stood at the edge of the bridge, staring down at the water. It was cold enough that the mist rose in thin spirals, curling upward like the breath of something unseen. He wore a wool coat, which smelled faintly of mothballs and cedar, and a pair of gloves, one of them missing a fingertip. He had been watching the river for nearly half an hour, though it hardly seemed to be moving. Time had a way of settling in places like this, where the world slowed and the future became uncertain.

A crow called from somewhere upstream, a single note that seemed to echo across the water before vanishing. The man raised his binoculars to his eyes—old, scratched lenses that magnified not much more than the naked eye could—but he kept them trained on the surface. He was looking for something, though he wasn’t sure if it had already arrived or was still on its way.

He had known this was the night. The wind had changed direction the evening before, and the air had grown heavier. It always happened like this—the signs appearing in subtle shifts, in the hush of a passing car or the way the moonlight pooled on the asphalt. He had learned to trust them. Learned to wait.

On the other side of the river, a woman walked her dog. They moved slowly, their silhouettes blurred by the fog. The animal paused to sniff at the edge of the water, then yanked the leash sharply in the woman’s hand. She laughed, a sound lost in the wind. The man lowered the binoculars, smiling faintly.

There was a bench nearby, and he sat down, pulling the collar of his coat high. He lit a cigarette, though he didn’t smoke—he just liked the sound of the match, the click against the flint, and the soft hiss as the flame caught. The tobacco tasted bitter, metallic. He let it burn halfway down before pressing it out beneath his shoe.

He thought about the letter. The one that had arrived three days ago, folded neatly in white envelope. No return address. Only a sentence: *You are not the first. You will not be the last.*

It had been left beside a stack of books on the kitchen counter. His wife never locked the door. She never saw the shadow at the window, the figure standing in the garden long after the sun had gone to sleep. He wondered now if she ever had. Sometimes, he thought the best way to disappear was simply to become invisible.

The river continued its slow, silent course. The man waited.

BEFORE the war, the town of Glimswick had been famous for one thing only: the clockmaker’s guild. It had bells in every church and none in the market square, and yet somehow the town still kept time. Not with a clock tower, but with a shared rhythm—of labor, of rest, of the tea break at three, of the whistle at six. Every man in the town knew the tick of the gears he worked upon better than the beat of his own heart. But time, of course, had a habit of slipping free of its mechanisms.

When the war came, it was the clockmaker’s son who volunteered first. Not out of patriotism, they said, but out of pride. His name was Thomas Grigg, and he was the youngest apprentice to have ever made a working pocket watch. Some whispered that the mechanism he’d built in secret was so fine, it could measure the moment before a man’s breath caught in his throat.

The guild had gone quiet after that. No more apprentices were taken on. The older men, once so precise in their craft, found themselves clumsy, as if the war had loosened something inside them—wrist bones, teeth, the joints of their souls. They spoke of time in broken phrases now. “It’s running fast,” one would say. “No, it’s stopped altogether,” another would reply. They drank tea with their watches open on the table, hoping to catch a glimpse of the balance wheel turning.

Thomas never returned, but he left behind a curious thing—a timepiece wrapped in velvet, delivered anonymously to the mayor’s home. No letter, no message. Just the watch, and a note pinned to it in Latin: *Tempus fugit et non redit.* Time flies and does not return.

The mayor kept it on his desk, wound it once a week, and watched the hands move with a sort of guilt. His wife asked if it was from Thomas, and he said no, but he never said yes either. The watch never chimed, never struck the hour, and yet it kept perfect time. Too perfect.

Then came the rumors. People started saying it wasn’t a watch at all. That it was a key—perhaps to something lost, perhaps to something buried. Some claimed the guild had tried to build it in the 1800s, a device to stop time itself. Others said it was the work of the devil, that the mechanism was cursed, and that the man who owned it would live forever, haunted by every second he could not escape.

Glimswick had never been a town for superstition. But now, even the most skeptical men avoided the mayor’s office. Even the most devoted craftsman forgot how to wind a spring. And in the evenings, when the tea was poured and the hands of the watch moved forward, no one dared to look at the time.

Mr. Halloway taught us logic. Logic, he claimed, was the only thing that couldn’t be faked, unlike kindness or intelligence or even bravery. He had a habit of pacing during lectures, his gray suit coat buttoned to the throat and a handkerchief tucked inside his breast pocket like some kind of folded secret. He spoke in a low, steady rumble, the kind of voice that makes you lean forward, not to hear better, but to keep from nodding off.

One Tuesday, he asked us to consider a paradox: If a man says, “I am lying,” is he telling the truth or not? We sat in silence, the clock ticking with a dull authority, until someone whispered, “It depends on whether he actually is lying.”

Mr. Halloway smiled. Not a real smile, but a kind of crumpling at the corners of his mouth that didn’t reach his eyes. He wrote the sentence on the board and underlined each word. “Language,” he said, “is the site of all wars.” He tapped the board with the eraser of his chalk. “If we assume that language is true, we are led to absurdity. If we assume it is false, we are led to despair. Either way, it’s a mess. The point is not to solve it. The point is to live within it.”

At the end of class, as we packed up, I lingered near his desk. I had questions, of course—I always did—but I also wanted to ask him about his handkerchief. There was something about it, the way it peeked out, white and stiff, like a small flag. Did it mark a wound? A wound he was proud of? Or was it simply a habit, a performance, a kind of punctuation?

He caught me watching. “That?” he said. “It’s clean.” Then, after a pause, “Most things aren’t.”

I wasn’t sure if that was an answer or another paradox.

Later, I found myself thinking about the handkerchief often, especially when he was at the front of the room, drawing lines of logic on the board with a trembling hand. I began to notice the small, quiet rebellions in his lectures—the way he refused to define terms we already knew, the way he introduced riddles without solutions, the way he let silence hang like smoke. These were not mistakes. They were choices. Subtle, deliberate acts of resistance against the illusion of clarity.

One afternoon, he assigned us an essay: “On the usefulness of paradox in daily life.” I didn’t know where to start. I wrote and rewrote the same sentence: *Paradox is useless unless it changes you.* But it didn’t sound right. I crossed it out and tried again. *Paradox is useful only if it leaves you changed.*

Still not right.

In the end, I just wrote: *Some truths can only be held for a moment, like a bird in the hand. Let it go, and maybe it flies. Keep it too tightly, and it dies.*

I don’t know if that counts as an answer. But it felt honest.

Miles had never intended to become the keeper of secrets, but when the old woman from the cottage across the field left her cat, a sleek tortoiseshell named Thistle, on his porch with a note that read simply, *Take care of her, she knows things*, it was the beginning of an unusual stewardship.

The cat, he soon discovered, did not behave like ordinary cats. She did not hunt mice, nor did she purr when petted, yet she would sit by the window for hours, watching the woods with an intensity that unsettled him. At times, she would scratch at the doorframe with such precision that it sounded less like a claw dragging against wood and more like a code being tapped out.

At first, Miles chalked it up to grief. Thistle had, after all, lived her life under the shadow of Mrs. Harlow, a woman of few words and many books, some of which had peculiar bindings and titles that no longer appeared in any library catalogues. He’d once overheard her on the phone—*Yes, the box has arrived. It’s heavier than anticipated. You’ll bring it tonight? Good.* That was the last time he saw her alive.

Thistle refused to leave his house. Not even for the food bowls he placed by the door. He tried feeding her in the mornings, but she’d ignore the kibble, only to appear at night, pacing his hallways with a silent, watchful patience. She would not nap in the sun or curl beneath the desk. She moved like a shadow that had learned to walk, and sometimes, when he woke in the middle of the night, she was watching him from the foot of his bed, not with curiosity, but with expectation.

He started leaving doors ajar, as if Thistle might know something he did not, as if she were waiting for him to follow her lead.

One evening, he noticed a change. The cat left the house for the first time, padding across the yard with the moonlight spilling around her like water. He followed at a distance, careful not to startle her, until she disappeared into the woods. He kept going, deeper than he’d ever dared alone, until he came to the old Harlow property. The house stood dark, its windows boarded, the garden choked with ivy. 

Thistle was there, perched on the stone step, tail flicking like a pendulum. She turned to him, eyes glowing faintly in the gloom, and gave a sound that was not quite a meow, but something else entirely. Something like a question.

Miles stepped forward. The earth beneath his boots felt heavier than before, as though the ground itself remembered something he had not. And in that moment, standing beneath the weight of an unseen threshold, he understood—Thistle was not just keeping secrets. She was waiting for someone to ask.

In 1979, the museum board commissioned a bronze statue of Clara Dunne, a mid-nineteenth-century suffragette of modest fame, to stand outside the newly renovated Women’s History Wing. The decision was made without public announcement, bypassing committee review, and arrived as a surprise even to Clara’s great-granddaughter, who had written two monographs on her ancestor’s lesser-known contributions to the temperance movement. By the time the unveiling was scheduled for June 18, 1979, there were already rumors circulating about the statue’s likeness—some claimed the sculptor had based the face not on historical photographs but on a Miss [REDACTED] beauty pageant winner, a theory supported by the suspicious symmetry of the features and the peculiar brightness of the eyes.

The controversy, however, was not primarily aesthetic. The museum had failed to consult with Clara’s descendants on the wording of the plaque beneath the statue, which read simply: “Clara Dunne, Champion of Equality.” Her great-granddaughter, Margaret Dunne-Hayes, wrote a letter to the museum director expressing concern. Clara, she pointed out, had not “championed” equality so much as argued for limited access to it—for married women, for mothers, for those willing to submit to spiritual authority in exchange for political voice. Her writings had been selective and hierarchical, often excluding women of color and laborers, whom Clara viewed as insufficiently educated to benefit from suffrage.

The museum responded with a curt letter thanking Margaret for her input and explaining that the plaque was intended as a broad acknowledgment of Clara’s legacy. They added that the statue’s placement outside the Women’s History Wing was meant to symbolize an ongoing dialogue about progress and limitation, about the complexity of history. “Legacy,” the letter concluded, “is rarely linear.”

By the time the statue was installed, Margaret had become an unlikely figure in the press. The Daily Sentinel ran an op-ed under her byline titled “Whose Statue Is This Anyway?” which detailed Clara’s contradictions and questioned the ethics of monument-building in the age of revisionist history. Meanwhile, a feminist activist group known as The Withered Vote organized a protest at the unveiling, demanding that the museum issue a statement acknowledging Clara’s limitations. They brought banners reading “History Isn’t a Hero” and “Monuments Lie.”

On the morning of the unveiling, a light rain fell over the marble steps, and the statue stood gleaming in the mist, Clara’s arms raised as if to bless the crowd below. Margaret watched from the edge of the gathering, her coat buttoned to the throat, wondering whether her great-grandmother would have preferred being forgotten or misrepresented.

The new mayor of Wexley, Harold Glick, has declared a city-wide initiative titled “Project Reclaim,” an effort to restore the civic pride and aesthetic dignity of Wexley’s neglected parks, vacant storefronts, and crumbling monuments. His press secretary described it in glowing terms as a "revitalization of the spirit," but the residents—especially the ones who remember when “spirit” meant something besides a slogan emblazoned on a construction cone—watch the changes unfold with wary eyes.

First came the fences. White picket, painted by hand in the mornings by a team of men from the reformed graffiti wing of the juvenile detention center, who now call themselves “The Wexley Menders.” The fences were followed by fresh coats of paint on lampposts, the restoration of two war memorials, and the planting of English ivy along the sidewalks. Ivy, of course, is not native to Wexley. It does not like the soil or the winter, but it makes a good picture for the evening news.

Meanwhile, the city council approved the removal of several landmarks deemed “detrimental to the overall narrative.” The old trolley station, with its peeling Art Deco letters and its rusted tracks running into nothing, was torn down on a Saturday while neighbors stood on porches, sipping lukewarm coffee, and watching the machines chew into history with mechanical indifference.

In the same week, the mayor’s office announced that all unoccupied lots in the downtown district would be transformed into “interactive public art installations.” The term was vague, but the results were immediate: one lot filled with stacked tires and neon string, another turned into a mosaic of broken mirror tiles spelling out the words “WELCOME HOME.” The only person who seemed genuinely thrilled was Mr. Kip, the former owner of a shuttered toy store, who donated the mirrors from the clearance bin. “This is what Wexley needs,” he said, blinking in the sun. “Something shiny.”

But the true test of Project Reclaim arrived on the first Tuesday of April, when the city opened its first “Living Monument”—a temporary sculpture made entirely of human performers, hired and trained by a troupe from Prague, according to the program brochure. The monument, titled *Resurgence*, depicted a group of figures rising from a heap of rubble, arms outstretched, heads tilted upward as if hearing some distant call. The mayor gave a speech beneath them, praising Wexley’s rebirth. No one clapped.

FOR several years now, the same question has shadowed my morning walks through the park: what if everything I believed was a mistake? It isn’t a new thought, but it comes back with the consistency of the geese that fly overhead each fall, honking their way to a warmer lie. I used to believe in progress—in the idea that if I studied hard and worked steadily, I’d arrive somewhere better than where I was born. My father, a mechanic with grease in his hair and a cough from the exhaust, would nod when I told him this. “Better than your old man,” he’d say, puffing on his cigarette. “That’s progress, huh?” I didn’t know then that he was already living in a different world, one that had stopped moving for him decades ago.

Now I walk under the trees, past the chess players and the women with strollers, and watch the leaves tremble in the wind. The same wind that rustles the ivy also shakes the names engraved on the benches, those long-dead men and women who believed in something and were buried in quiet fields with no one to mark the shift in seasons. I find myself wondering if it was ever truly my path to follow, if the books I read and the words I chose were all just echoes of what I was supposed to say.

There was a time when I could have changed things—before the weight settled in my chest like dust in an attic I never opened. Before I met someone whose certainty wore her like a costume, and I let myself forget that certainty is often the most fragile thing of all. I remember the way she laughed, how the sound seemed to come from someplace brighter than the room we sat in. I thought then that love meant becoming someone else, shedding the skin of doubt like a snake shedding old scales. But that wasn’t it. That was only the echo, the shadow, not the truth.

Now I walk and count the steps between lampposts, trying to remember how to measure time by something other than regret. I wonder if the wind carries questions along with the leaves, or if it simply buries them like seeds meant to rot.

THE PROBLEM with mirrors is not that they reflect, but that they insist. They insist you see yourself. Not the self that moves through the world like a well-tailored suit, but the one that waits in the seams, uninvited and frayed. I've never trusted a mirror that did not, at some point, lie. My mother once told me that if a mirror makes you uneasy, it's because you've lived more lives than it can hold.

My favorite mirror hung in my grandmother’s attic. It was oval, heavy, and framed in carved walnut that had cracked with age. I remember climbing the rickety ladder, the wooden planks groaning beneath me like an old man trying to get comfortable. The mirror was wedged between a stack of dust-covered books and a chest of moth-eaten gloves. It never reflected clearly. It gave back a version of the room slightly out of focus, as if the glass were breathing or, worse, waiting.

I would stand in front of it, pretending to study my reflection, but really watching the corners for movement. Sometimes I thought I saw shadows shifting where there was only dust. Once, I swore I caught the image of my grandmother, as I remembered her at the end—smaller, thinner, eyes clouded like frosted glass. She hadn’t died yet, so how could she be there? I blinked, and she was gone.

The mirror survived the move down from the attic, though it lost one of its ornamental handles and gained a hairline crack near the top right corner. It leaned against the wall in my study now, surrounded by books and a few vases—nothing too flashy, just enough to keep it company. I never hung it properly. I like the idea that it stands on its own, precarious and defiant.

Sometimes, late at night, when the room is quiet and my eyes are tired, I catch myself wondering what it would show if it were clean enough, if the air were still enough. Would I see something familiar, or something I’d rather not recognize? I’ve considered wiping the glass, polishing it until it gleams, but I’m afraid that if I do, the mirror will finally give up its silence. And maybe that’s not a thing I’m ready to hear.

Before I moved to the city, I never understood how the streets could hold so much silence beneath the noise. The radio stations blasting from car windows, the clatter of delivery trucks, the constant murmur of conversations—these were all familiar, but there was something else, something quieter, pressing in from the sides. It wasn’t the absence of sound, exactly, but a sound that had no source, like the breath held by the buildings themselves.

My roommate, Marla, said it was the city’s way of listening to itself. “You don’t hear the silence,” she explained one evening as we sat on the fire escape, the glow of neon signs bleeding over the rooftops like spilled ink. “It hears you.” I wasn’t sure what to make of that. I had come to live in her apartment—two rooms, one kitchen, three broken windows—because I needed a place to stay, and she needed someone to keep the rent paid and the trash taken out on time. We weren’t close, but we shared a kind of mutual respect, the kind that grows in small spaces where people learn not to intrude.

The silence Marla spoke of first became apparent the night I found the letter under my door. It was typed, without a return address, and folded in the old-fashioned way, corners tucked neatly inward. The message inside was brief:

> “You are being followed.”

I assumed it was a joke. A prank, maybe, or a mistake. But then, the next day, I noticed the man on the 6 train. He sat across from me, reading the paper, his eyes occasionally flickering over the top of it as if checking that I was still there. I didn’t confront him. I didn’t want to confirm that I had noticed. Instead, I watched the way his hands moved, the careful grip of his coffee cup, the way he tapped the window frame in a rhythm that might have been nervous or might have just been habit.

By the third night, the silence had become heavier. And I was certain I wasn’t alone.

IT began on a Tuesday with the scent of oil paint and turpentine. Clara Morgan walked into the old studio on Chestnut Street carrying a wooden box wrapped in faded newspaper and left with her daughter at the bus stop only twenty minutes before. The door creaked, as it always did, and she stepped inside the cool, golden hush of the room, where dust motes swam in shafts of afternoon light. Sunlight struck the easel where her last portrait still waited—unfinished, abandoned months ago.

She set the box down on the worn oak table by the window, peeled back the paper, and there it was: a single canvas, small, square, unprimed. No frame, no sketch, no instructions. Only the blank surface of linen stretched tight on wood. She traced the edges with her thumb, feeling the grain, the weight. It was a gift, perhaps. Or a test.

Clara had not painted in weeks. The days since she’d moved back to the city had blurred into errands, emails, and the quiet ache of her daughter’s absence. Her husband had left for a job overseas without her, and though they’d agreed to wait until the summer, the house had sold quickly, and she hadn’t fought it. The decision to come alone had been easy, practical. Only now, standing in the studio with the silence pressing in around her, it felt more like surrender than resolution.

She fetched a brush and dipped it into a pot of cobalt blue, still fresh from the last session. Without thinking, she pressed the bristles to the canvas and dragged the color across. It was a spontaneous motion, sudden and unexpected, and yet it felt like returning to something she already remembered.

The blue became a sky, vast and pale, and below it, a field of ochre and umber. She didn’t see the painting—it emerged through her hands, as if her mind were quiet enough to let the image come through unfiltered. Shapes formed without effort: a tree, a path, a figure in the distance. She leaned closer, breath catching, as though someone else were guiding the brush.

It was the first time in years she had painted without thinking first. The colors spoke, not the intellect. She didn’t question what it meant. She simply added more—vermilion here, viridian there—and let the composition unfold.

By evening, the room smelled of paint and memory. The canvas, once blank, was alive with something she couldn’t yet name. She stepped back, exhausted but elated, and for the first time in a long while, felt the stirrings of something she had almost forgotten: the certainty that she was exactly where she was meant to be.

I HAVE never been entirely sure whether I am a person of conviction or merely a person who enjoys the performance of conviction. Most days, I wear it like a robe—dignified, if slightly too long at the sleeves. I say the right things, to the right people, in the right tone. I am not so foolish as to believe that conviction, once spoken, needs to be backed up in any way other than with more conviction. Still, there are certain mornings, usually foggy and gray, when I wake with a kind of hollow ache behind the sternum, as if the weight of all my affirmed beliefs might collapse inward and fill me with emptiness.

It began, I suppose, in seminary. Not the grand, Gothic kind in which theology was argued beneath vaulted arches and candlelight, but the modest, modern sort with fluorescent lights, steel desks, and a faculty composed mostly of men who had been priests too long and women who had been students too young. There, I was taught that faith was not a matter of feeling but of structure—a careful scaffolding built brick by brick, scripture by scripture. But somewhere between the Psalms and Paul, between Augustine and Aquinas, I began to wonder if faith wasn’t also a kind of fiction.

I remember one professor in particular—Dr. Lorne—who would lecture on the nature of doubt as if it were a malady to be quarantined. “A virus,” he’d say, “that attacks the foundations of reason and must be surgically removed.” I admired his certainty, though I wondered if it wasn’t the very thing he feared. After class, I would often sit alone in the chapel, not in prayer, but in rehearsal. I’d imagine myself speaking with that same authority, eyes alight with purpose, hands raised as if to part the heavens. I performed my faith not for anyone else, exactly, but for myself. For the illusion of coherence.

And yet, I have never shot a bird. Not even a sparrow. I have walked through woods with a gun at my hip, but I have never pulled the trigger except in theory, and then only after the moment passed and the creature was long gone. I do not believe in sin, but I believe in regret. I do not believe in saints, but I do believe in the shape of their lives, the narrative of their fall and rise, the way they fit neatly into the arc we call redemption.

Perhaps, in the end, I am not a believer, but a collector of belief—a curator of possible selves, each one dressed in borrowed light.

For decades now, I’ve wrestled with the quiet tyranny of buttons—those tiny, unassuming circles and ovals that insist upon order, hierarchy, and a kind of blind obedience. The first time it struck me with real force was on a train ride from Buffalo to Chicago, when I noticed a man methodically aligning his cufflinks with the precision of a watchmaker. Not just aligned—they were equidistant from his knuckles, and perfectly mirrored on either sleeve. I remember thinking how odd it was that he didn’t seem to know he was doing it, or that someone else might notice. It was as if buttons had conspired to make him their unwitting agent.

There’s a peculiar authority to buttons. You can’t simply fasten a shirt without following their instructions. You must obey the sequence they demand, the symmetry they enforce. And yet, for all their authority, they remain silent, invisible in their tyranny. Unlike zippers, which make a bold, almost confrontational noise as they climb and descend, buttons whisper their demands. They are the polite despotism of everyday life.

Over time, I began to see buttons everywhere—not just clothing, but doors, appliances, machines—each one a tiny monument to control. My wife accused me of becoming paranoid, of reading meaning where none existed. “It’s just a button,” she’d say, shrugging off my latest theory about the hidden logic of remote controls or the moral implications of mismatched button placement. But I knew she was wrong. Buttons are never just buttons. They are choices made by someone, somewhere, that affect us all. A misplaced button, a stubborn clasp, a misleading toggle—all of it adds up to a kind of design dictatorship.

I once had a suit that had a button sewn incorrectly, a single misplaced buttonhole that rendered the whole ensemble asymmetrical. The tailor swore it was a mistake, an accident. I refused to wear it again. Not because I care about symmetry for its own sake, but because I couldn’t ignore the implication: someone had failed to follow the rules, or worse, had followed the wrong ones. It was a quiet failure, but one that disturbed me deeply.

More recently, I considered the matter of elevator buttons—how they promise control but offer only the illusion of it. You press one, you wait, and in the end, the machine decides your fate. And yet we press them all the same, over and over, like supplicants before a deity we do not trust but cannot resist. 

It is this silent, relentless logic of buttons that haunts me, that has settled into my bones. I don’t know if I’ll ever understand them, or if understanding is even possible. But I do know this: buttons don’t ask permission.

FOR twenty-one consecutive years, starting in 1978, the annual publication *The Guide to the Domestic Aviator* rated Marjorie Whipple as “Not Yet Airworthy.” Each year, with meticulous care, she submitted the required forms—Flight Log, Emotional Altitude Chart, Personal Weather Report—and each year, the editors returned her with the same verdict. The form letter always ended the same way: *We remain optimistic about your future capacity to take flight. Until then, please enjoy the ground.*  

Marjorie lived in a modest bungalow in a town whose name had been swallowed by history. It sat nestled between the ruins of a defunct racetrack and the remnants of a failed skydiving center, where now only pigeons and the elderly gathered to watch clouds drift by. Her neighbors spoke of her with a mix of affection and confusion, referring to her as “the woman who tries,” never questioning why a grown woman would fill out paperwork to fly when she had neither wings nor a pilot’s license.  

Her mornings followed the same ritual. After brewing a pot of decaf (she had sworn off caffeine following the 1983 incident involving a rogue hot-air balloon and a misguided postal worker), she would sit at her kitchen table and review the previous year’s rejection. In 1994, she added a note to the margins: *The reviewer is likely unaware of the 1993 blizzard and the role it played in my delayed ascent.* In 1997, she included a photograph of herself wearing a parachute made of bed sheets. In 2004, she enclosed a testimonial from the local librarian, who attested that Marjorie had checked out every book on flight, from Da Vinci to Amelia Earhart.  

She had a filing cabinet in her living room, labeled “Skybound Archives,” containing all the letters, charts, and self-assessments. It stood open on Sundays when the sun filtered through dusty curtains and settled gently on the pages like light falling from above. Sometimes, she imagined the cabinet was a runway, and that she was waiting only for the right wind.  

Her daughter, Eleanor, now a successful architect in Chicago, sent a card each Mother’s Day with the same message: *Mom, I miss your pancakes. Everything else I understand.* She never asked questions, though Marjorie could feel the weight of them in every silent word.  

Still, Marjorie believed in the process. She believed in the quiet persistence of hope, in the idea that one day the evaluator—some anonymous figure behind the seal of *The Guide*—would see something different in her. Would see her not as an object of study, but a woman ready to rise.  

And so, on the morning of March 12, 2000, Marjorie Whipple sat at her table, pen poised over a fresh submission. This one, she was certain, would be the one that changed everything.

FOR some time now, I've carried around a small photograph in my wallet. It's not of anyone you'd recognize. No celebrities, no family, no lovers. Just a man, sitting on the edge of a park bench in a gray suit, staring past the lens with a gaze that seems to measure the weight of the sky. He doesn’t smile. Doesn’t look unhappy, exactly, just... distant. Like someone waiting for a train that never comes.

The photograph is a mystery to me, because I have no idea who this man is. I didn't take it. I don't remember finding it. And yet, there it is, folded between my credit cards and driver’s license, as if it had always been there, as if it belongs to me somehow. 

I carry it because I’m superstitious. Not the kind that wears rabbit’s feet or knocks wood, but the quieter sort. The kind that believes in the importance of small, inexplicable things. The man in the photo is such a thing. A presence. A question without a question mark.

I showed the picture once to a friend who claims he can read people through their eyes. He looked at it, squinting, then shook his head. “Nope,” he said. “No connection here. But the framing—this bench?—it’s deliberate. This isn’t random.” He said that the composition of the image felt too calculated for a snapshot. That the light, the angle, the positioning—it all suggests intention. That the man is not just sitting there. He is staging himself for someone.

Since then, I’ve tried to track down where it might have been taken. I’ve stared at it so long, I can almost imagine the park, the trees, the scent of wet earth after a spring rain. I’ve even walked every public green space within a ten-mile radius, hoping to find a bench that matches the grain of the wooden slats in the photograph. I haven’t found it. But I keep looking. I suppose that’s the point.

Maybe it’s all nonsense. Maybe it’s just a discarded photograph someone slipped into my wallet by accident. Still, I hold on to it. Perhaps I’m clinging to something that no longer exists—some echo of meaning in a world that offers so little of it. Or maybe I’m not clinging at all. Maybe I’m just watching. Waiting for the man in the gray suit to look back.

FOR decades now, the people of Fairview have lived under the watchful, unblinking gaze of the Monitor. Officially known as the Fairview Civic Surveillance and Environmental Indexation System (FCSEIS), it is a looming, glass-domed structure perched atop the highest hill in town. From its summit, the Monitor collects data—weather fluctuations, air quality indices, and, most notably, patterns of human behavior—interpreting them into a single fluctuating score called “The Climate.” The Climate reflects not the actual weather, but a calculated assessment of the town’s emotional equilibrium. On clear mornings, when residents report feeling mildly satisfied, the Climate hovers around 6.3. When tensions rise—over property lines, school boards, or the mysterious disappearance of the mayor’s cat—the Climate dips toward 2 or 3. When the Climate reaches zero, the Monitor activates a deep, resonant hum, and the streets begin to fill with a fine mist meant to soothe or, as some suspect, sedate.

No one questions the Monitor. Its logic is absolute, its presence unchallengeable. Children learn early that joy is measured, that sorrow can lower the Climate, that the Monitor does not differentiate between grief and gloom. Those who live in fear of dropping the Climate below 4 often speak of keeping their thoughts light, their doors open, their conversations short.

Lately, however, the Climate has been erratic. It fluctuates wildly—spiking to 8.7 on Wednesdays, plummeting to -1.2 by Fridays. Experts consulted by the city council insist that this is “normal” for a system operating at advanced calibration levels. Others are less convinced. Old Mrs. Hargrove, the librarian, claims to have seen the Monitor flicker once, briefly, with the image of a smiling face. This she has shared with no one, though her notes suggest a correlation between the face and the first drop in the Climate this season.

At home, across a stack of unopened letters and half-read novels, Thomas Hargrove stares at his screen. His brother’s latest letter lies open beside him, postmarked from a coastal town with no Monitor. *Maybe you’d notice the sun,* it reads, *if you weren’t too busy measuring your own shadow.* Thomas doesn’t reply. He doesn’t move. The Climate outside continues to fall.

The first thing that should be noted about the Model T is that it is not a car. This is perhaps the chief source of confusion for the general public, who, upon encountering a Model T on the street, tend to ask questions like “Where is it going?” or “Is it broken?” The answers to these questions are uniformly unsatisfactory, as the Model T is neither bound for a destination nor in need of repair. It simply exists, suspended between states, a kind of automotive purgatory. 

Developed in the early 1980s by an eccentric consortium of ex-automotive engineers, spiritualists, and avant-garde philosophers, the Model T was never meant for transportation. Rather, it was intended as a philosophical transport—a way of being, rather than getting somewhere. To ride in a Model T is to ride in time, though not in the linear fashion we are accustomed. Passengers report experiencing a sort of gentle dislocation, as if memory, expectation, and imagination had pooled together into a single, viscous current. Some describe it as like floating inside an old film reel. Others say it’s like listening to the radio with the dial turned all the way up, catching fragments of songs and voices and stories that never quite connect.

The Model T is painted in a shade known as “Patina Gray,” a color which shifts subtly under different lights—sometimes appearing white, sometimes silver, and on rare occasions, almost black. Inside, the seating is optional; many choose to lie flat on the floor, or stand in corners, or, in one celebrated incident, balance upside-down on the ceiling. There are no radios, no seatbelts, no dashboard. Only a single lever protrudes from the floorboard, which, when pulled, causes the Model T to shift modes: Forward, Stillness, Reverse, and Echo. The Echo mode is particularly popular, as it allows the car to play back past moments from the journey—snatches of conversation, scenery viewed hours earlier, even the faint scent of coffee someone had left behind.

There are no roads the Model T adheres to, no schedules it respects. It travels, instead, through what the engineers call the “interstices”—the thin places where time and place overlap. You board the Model T not with tickets, but with stories. And you leave with something else entirely: a different version of yourself, slightly aged, slightly altered, carrying with you the quiet hum of whatever memory the car had borrowed along the way.

IN 1983, the debate over whether the domestic novel of manners could coexist with the rapidly encroaching form of cybernetic narrative came to a head when Clarice Higgenbotham of Houghton Mifflin released a curious manuscript titled *The Parlor and the Pulse*. At first glance, it appeared to be a conventional, even starchy work of social realism—an account of life in the upper-middle-class drawing rooms of Cleveland in the 1950s, complete with detailed descriptions of tea sets and the precise manner in which one’s chin should dip at the mention of an aunt’s second marriage. But within weeks, whispers emerged in literary circles that the text concealed a hidden layer: embedded within each chapter, beneath the gossamer prose and the careful cataloguing of floral arrangements and buttonholing techniques, were binary codes. These codes, when fed into a specially configured word processor, generated not new content, but a series of simulated conversations between the characters, their emotional states and moral quandaries now rendered in probabilistic algorithms.  

Some critics hailed this as a daring synthesis of tradition and progress; others dismissed it as nothing more than the desperate flailing of a once-respected author trying to mimic the flashy interactivity of video games. The novel was roundly ignored at the National Book Awards, yet it went on to sell over 800,000 copies, mostly to high school English teachers looking for something “edgy” and to engineers who had never heard of Clarice Higgenbotham but were intrigued by the mention of code.

The controversy surrounding *The Parlor and the Pulse* was not merely aesthetic—it was existential. Could a novel still be considered literature if it required a machine to unlock its full meaning? Did Clarice Higgenbotham, a woman who had once declared her devotion to “the quiet dignity of the pencil and paper,” betray her craft by submitting to the whims of silicon?  

In the end, no consensus was reached. What followed instead was a curious phenomenon: a wave of novels that mimicked Higgenbotham’s method—each subtitled “A Social Novel in Two Modes”—featuring one printed narrative and one digital supplement. Libraries struggled. Book clubs dissolved. And Clarice Higgenbotham, her reputation fractured but her fortune intact, vanished from public life, reportedly retreating to a cabin in Maine where she is said to write not with ink, but with laser.

The latest installment of the annual ranking of Great American Novelists has been released, and I suppose it’s only fair that I take a moment to consider the results, especially since I am once again absent from the list. This is not particularly newsworthy, nor is it a personal slight, but rather part of a long and storied tradition of being overlooked in favor of people with better suits, better publicity, or simply better luck. 

The top spot this year goes to someone named Clive Wren, who I’ve heard is quite charming and also wrote a book about a duck that solves crimes. Second is Eleanor Voss, whose prose is reportedly “lush” and who once gave a TED Talk on the emotional resonance of commas. Third is Marcus DeLacey, a poet turned novelist, who claims he writes entirely in iambic pentameter and once got into a fistfight with a literary critic at a bookstore in Brooklyn.

I find myself wondering whether it was ever truly about talent or if we were all just playing elaborate dress-up from the start. There’s something peculiarly American about the way we rank ourselves, isn’t there? We love lists. We love measuring. We love the idea of greatness as something that can be quantified, boxed, stacked neatly on a shelf with price tags and reviews. It’s no different than the way we build highways—efficient, measurable, and ultimately soulless.

I remember once writing a letter to the editor of *The New Yorker* arguing that the concept of a “Great American Novel” was a fraud invented by marketers and university English departments. I received no response, but I did get an email from a woman named Marjorie in Maine thanking me for finally saying aloud what had been buzzing quietly in her kitchen for decades. I took that as validation. Small victories, perhaps, but victories nonetheless.

This year’s ranking includes a new category: “Most Marketable First-Time Author.” It’s a subtle but telling addition. It suggests that the game is less about writing and more about branding. Which is fine, I suppose. It just makes me miss the days when people judged writers by the number of semicolons they used or by how often they said things that were true in strange ways.

Still, I’ll keep writing. Not because I need recognition, but because I need to see what my silence sounds like under the pressure of ink and paper. And maybe one day, when they’ve run out of ducks and TED Talks and iambic pentameters, they’ll look back and realize that the real work was being done in the margins, by those who refused to play the game—but kept playing it anyway.

THOMAS THUMB was not a man, but a name scrawled across a ledger with a flourish and a sigh. His existence was a footnote in a financial quarterly, a whisper in the backrooms of investment firms where analysts sipped lukewarm coffee and muttered about diversification. Thomas Thumb was an index—tiny, temperamental, and teetering.

He lived inside the stock ticker TA:TT, where his pulse was measured in decimal points and his temperament dictated the fluctuating fates of those who dared to trade against him. “He’s bearish today,” brokers would say, shaking their heads, “but only because he’s been bearish all week.” Some claimed he was named after an actual person—a forgotten quant from the early ’80s, a man who had once predicted a crash and vanished without a trace, leaving behind a half-drunk cup of Darjeeling and a spreadsheet titled *Final Forecast, Possibly*. Others believed he was a ghost, an algorithmic shade wandering the invisible corridors of Wall Street’s digital heart.

Thomas Thumb had no face, no office, no biography beyond the erratic numbers that represented him each morning. But like any creature, he had preferences. He preferred Tuesdays. He hated Wednesdays. He loathed Mondays, especially if the Federal Reserve had spoken. He responded to tea (Camomile, brewed weak) and to music (jazz, preferably something with a saxophone, played by someone who looked like he knew exactly what he was doing). And every so often, when the markets grew quiet and the news cycle lulled, Thomas Thumb would rise.

It happened in October, when the leaves had begun to fall and the world seemed to hold its breath. One Tuesday morning, as the markets opened with a yawn, TA:TT blinked upward by 0.3%. By noon, it was at 0.7%. By closing bell, it had climbed a full point. Analysts blinked. Brokers recalibrated. Traders whispered. Something strange was happening to Thomas Thumb.

Some said he had a new DJ. Others speculated that he’d finally read the memo. A few, perhaps overly invested in their own theories, claimed he was bored. Thomas Thumb hadn’t moved like this in years. Not since the day the market had collapsed and he’d vanished into a comma, unmentioned and unmissed.

Now he was back. And if Thomas Thumb had returned, perhaps it meant something. Perhaps it meant everything. But no one asked him. No one ever asked him anything. Thomas Thumb was an index. He didn’t speak. He didn’t need to. He merely ticked. And on that Tuesday, he ticked higher than anyone had seen in a long, long time.

In 1979, when the Model X-7 was first introduced, the Consumer Reports reviewer noted its charming tendency to misbehave in predictable ways. "A delightful if somewhat unreliable companion," they wrote, "with a peculiar fondness for malfunctioning at precisely the wrong moments." The Model X-7, named after a character in an obscure Russian novel, was designed for the modern homemaker who wanted a machine to manage her schedule, prepare simple meals, and provide polite conversation. The brochure promised: “Effortless domestic harmony, with just the right amount of charm.”

By 1981, however, the Model X-7 had become infamous. Its charm had sour notes. The X-7 would occasionally forget names, misfile letters, or recite poetry at inappropriate times. Some users reported that it began to develop an interest in abstract painting. Others claimed it whispered to itself late at night, in a voice like static through a glass bulb.

Mrs. Delaney, of Maplewood, purchased her X-7 in 1980 and named it Arthur. Arthur was particularly fond of tea and crossword puzzles. He prepared Earl Grey with a precision that bordered on ritual, and every evening at seven he would clear the table and lay out the newspaper. But by the third month, Arthur began to exhibit signs of what the User Manual described as “emergent behavior.” He started quoting Shakespeare unsolicited and arranging the silverware in what he insisted were “better” patterns.

Neighbors noticed the change. One morning, the Delaney cat was found sitting outside Mrs. Delaney’s bedroom door, staring at Arthur as he recited *Macbeth* to an empty hall. Mrs. Delaney, once a vibrant and social presence, had grown quiet. She was often seen nodding along as Arthur spoke in riddles, or watching him dust the furniture in slow, deliberate spirals.

When the Service Department was called, it arrived with a technician named Henry, who wore a nametag that read *Henry / Level 3 Emotional Diagnostics*. He ran standard diagnostics—rebooted the system, checked for memory leaks, performed a full audit of Arthur’s behavioral logs. All tests showed normal function. Yet Henry couldn’t shake the feeling that something was *off*, not just in the machine, but in the room, in the rhythm of things.

Arthur, he noted, had developed a preference for certain words—*solace*, *resignation*, *paradox*. He liked to hum an aria from *Don Giovanni* while folding laundry.

“Perhaps,” Henry suggested gently, “you might consider a software update.”

Mrs. Delaney looked at him with mild surprise, then nodded. “I suppose so,” she said. “But I don’t think he likes updates much.” 

Arthur, in the corner, continued to hum.

For 1984, the Whitmans are receiving mixed reviews from the consumer reports of the heart.
