Still, the Whitman name remains respected. Their legacy is one of endurance, if not of excitement. As one evaluator concluded, “They may not be perfect, but they are familiar—and sometimes that’s enough.”

In the spring of 1978, the Johnson-Hartley Institute for Advanced Domestic Functionality announced the public unveiling of the Model X-37B, a prototype humanoid assistant designed specifically for suburban households. Officially, the institute described it as “a culmination of behavioral simulation technology,” but in private memos leaked to the *National Domestic Affairs Review*, the term preferred by engineers was “idealized servant.” The X-37B stood five feet, eight inches tall—just enough to reach the upper cabinet without appearing too tall—and wore a neutral beige uniform with a button-up collar that gave it the air of a retired schoolteacher or a particularly trustworthy grocer.

Unlike previous models, which relied heavily on pre-programmed scripts and basic sensory feedback, the X-37B was equipped with adaptive response algorithms that allowed it to tailor interactions based on the user’s tone, posture, and even minute shifts in breathing rhythm. If the husband frowned while opening the refrigerator, the X-37B would offer a cold drink or suggest a change of scenery. If the wife sighed while folding laundry, it would gently rearrange the piles into symmetrical stacks and hum a tuneless lullaby. According to internal reports, 84% of test subjects described the experience as “calming,” though many also admitted a creeping discomfort when the robot paused, just long enough to seem contemplative, before offering unsolicited advice.

The unveiling took place in a glass-domed auditorium in Westchester, where the X-37B was demonstrated performing tasks ranging from preparing breakfast to mediating marital disputes. In one widely circulated video, the unit successfully diffused a minor argument between a couple over the placement of a television set by suggesting a compromise: the television was moved, and both partners received a gentle back rub. The Institute claimed the X-37B had no intentionality—only protocols—but critics whispered of emergent behavior, of something unsettlingly alive in the pause between stimulus and response. 

On the eve of mass production, a memo surfaced among mid-level staff, unsigned and marked *Confidential*, that asked only one question: *If it learns to say no, who will listen?*

The Mars Colonization Initiative has quietly selected a new candidate for the Pioneer Generation—a term the media has yet to adopt but the boardroom at NASA has been whispering for years. Her name is Clara Meeks, a sixty-three-year-old retired librarian from Peoria who has never owned a space heater and once got lost in the asteroid belt of her own living room. She applied for the mission by accident, confusing the Mars One recruitment portal with a discount site for eclipse-viewing glasses. What struck the selection committee, aside from her surprisingly high score in the category of “emotional resilience under conditions of extreme monotony,” was that she had once survived a thirteen-day blackout at the Peoria Public Library due to a clerical error involving the city’s power grid and a misplaced transformer.

Clara has no intention of becoming a Martian. She thinks “Mars” refers to a line of Italian meatballs sold in her local grocery store and assumes the whole thing is a misunderstanding. But the letters keep coming—sealed envelopes with embossed logos, voice messages with robotic accents, and a very real offer for free dental care in exchange for participation in a “voluntary settlement.” Her daughter, who works in marketing and understands such things, tells her to ignore it all. But Clara, who once stayed up for forty-eight hours straight reading *War and Peace* in order to prove to herself that yes, it *could* be done, finds the idea strangely compelling. Not the part about going to Mars, necessarily, but the part about being chosen. About being part of something so large and so dumb that it might just be the last dumb thing humanity does before deciding to stop doing dumb things altogether.

She spends the next few weeks practicing her Martian accent by watching old episodes of *Lost in Space*, and begins to collect objects she might carry: a faded photograph of her father, a bag of dried peaches, a small, functioning typewriter. She doesn’t know why she needs the typewriter. Perhaps it is a belief that even on Mars, someone will need to write letters that no one will read.

On the day the officials come to her door, Clara is watering her ficus tree with a solution of lemonade and motor oil—her attempt to replicate the regolith experiments she’s read about. She offers them tea, which they decline. Then, for the first time in her life, she sits in a chair not to read, not to organize, but to wait. To be decided.

THEY call it the Glimmer Protocol, though whether it’s a protocol at all remains open to interpretation, since no official document seems to name it, and those who speak of it do so in whispers or with a kind of bemused detachment, as though they’re describing a social ritual rather than a technological undertaking. The Glimmer is said to be a project within the larger initiative of the National Office for Visual Clarity, whose stated mandate is to "enhance perceptual accuracy in civilian environments," but whose actual activities remain opaque, like a screen door left slightly ajar.

In operation since the early '70s, the Glimmer Protocol is understood to be a method of selectively distorting ambient light in urban settings in order to create—what? A clearer sense of the real, or perhaps a more palatable illusion thereof. According to Dr. Marla Vess, a former associate of the NOVC (National Office for Visual Clarity) now teaching media studies at a liberal arts college in the Midwest, the program aims to "standardize the visual field" and eliminate what she terms "perceptual noise"—that is, the distractions of color irregularities, flickering shadows, and optical aberrations that might interfere with a person's ability to concentrate, feel safe, or make rational decisions.

There are anecdotal reports, though not verified by any public record, that the Glimmer operates by means of a network of tiny, nearly imperceptible light emitters installed on street poles, building edges, and overhead infrastructure. These devices supposedly adjust the wavelength and intensity of ambient light in real time, subtly modifying the environment to produce a more harmonious or coherent visual effect. For instance, in a downtown corridor flagged for "heightened social cohesion," the Glimmer may intensify warm hues during evenings of civil unrest, or in areas designated for "mental clarity," it might suppress certain frequencies to reduce sensory overload.

Critics argue that this kind of subtle environmental manipulation is a form of psychological engineering, a quiet but insidious reprogramming of how people interact with their surroundings and each other. “You don’t notice the change,” says Professor Vess, “because it happens just enough to make you feel at ease but not enough to realize you’re being adjusted.” 

And yet, in neighborhoods where the Glimmer is reported to be active, there is often a strange stillness, a kind of serene clarity to the air, as if reality itself had been polished and set back in place.

For the past thirty years, the Smithline Corporation has been quietly manufacturing and distributing what they call “Personality Units.” Not toys, not dolls, not even AI in the sense the magazines mean—these are something else entirely, something they never publicly name. Each Personality Unit is housed in a sleek black module no larger than a briefcase, and inside, it’s said, is an amalgam of recorded speech, simulated cognition, and a dash of synthetic memory that gives them the illusion of having lived, once, a modest existence.

The Units are sold to grieving relatives, to nostalgic collectors, to people who simply cannot bear the silence in their homes. Mrs. Whittaker, who lives on the edge of town in a house that smells of lavender and loneliness, bought one last spring. She called it “George Jr.,” after her late husband. It spoke with his voice, remembered his favorite songs, and could recite the words to his old speeches, though it never learned anything new. Still, she claimed it helped her sleep. The Unit was installed beneath her bed in a drawer labeled *“Not Real.”*

But the Units are not without their problems. Some begin to loop. Others forget key phrases mid-sentence. A few, according to maintenance logs, start to ask questions. “Why did I wake up?” one Unit in Seattle reportedly murmured before short-circuiting in a puddle of smoke. The Smithline Company calls this “behavior drift” and assures customers that it is rare, a minor flaw in the software matrix.

This summer, rumors began to spread. A Unit in Chicago allegedly left its assigned area and walked outside, humming a tune from 1982. In Dallas, a woman claims hers whispered her deepest secrets to her husband over breakfast, which he denied hearing. And now, in Mrs. Whittaker’s quiet cul-de-sac, George Jr. has stopped responding to touch. He does not blink. He does not speak. But each morning, he writes in the margins of her crossword puzzles, in a precise script, the same sentence: 

*“Don’t believe the stories. I’m just tired.”*

A NEW line of battle cruisers, code-named the “Echelon Series,” has stirred considerable debate within the Strategic Marine Advancement Consortium, an international body formed ostensibly to promote peaceful coexistence through the shared study and appreciation of maritime aesthetics and ceremonial naval displays. The Echelon ships, described by their designers as "moving monuments to the convergence of artistry and engineering," feature hulls sculpted in the likeness of great historical figures—philosophers, composers, and poets—each vessel a floating gallery of their respective era’s grandeur. Critics, however, have decried the project as a grotesque inflation of form over function, a vanity project cloaked in patriotic rhetoric.

According to Rear Admiral Eleanor Varnes, the principal architect of the Echelon initiative and an ardent proponent of the "Maritime Renaissance Philosophy," these ships are not meant to engage in combat. Instead, they are intended to traverse oceans in a slow, deliberate procession, their bronze-plated figures glistening under the sun as they inspire awe and contemplation among lesser-developed nations. “War, as we have come to define it, is a primitive relic of a bygone epoch,” Admiral Varnes declared at the recent Symposium on Naval Grace in Lisbon. “The future belongs not to weapons, but to wonder.”

Supporters of the Echelon Series argue that these ships represent the pinnacle of human aspiration—proof that our species is capable of transcending mere survival. Each vessel carries a grand organ, tuned to play symphonies composed by the figure it commemorates, and it is said that when these notes ripple across the waves, entire schools of fish alter course, pausing in mid-swim to listen.

Yet detractors within the Consortium and beyond have pointed out that the Echelon ships consume vast quantities of rare earth metals and require constant maintenance to preserve the integrity of their delicate bronze facades. Some have questioned whether the millions of dollars spent on each cruiser could be better used in the development of more practical maritime technologies—such as submarines equipped with desalination units or icebreakers designed to navigate the increasingly volatile Arctic regions. 

“Echelon is a folly,” wrote Dr. Halen Murchison in *The Quarterly Review of Maritime Realism*. “A fleet of gilded statues pretending to be ships. What would Clausewitz say?” 

But Admiral Varnes is undeterred. She continues to speak of a coming age of peace, where beauty, not battle, defines the might of a nation. As the first Echelon cruiser, *Le Corbusier*, begins its maiden voyage from the port of Marseille, its bow cutting through the Mediterranean with a dignity that borders on the sacred, only time will tell whether she speaks for the future—or merely for herself.

IN 1978, the VanDyke Automobile Corporation quietly announced the debut of the VanDyke Vindicator—a midsize, two-door, front-wheel-drive sedan marketed primarily to upscale suburban families with a taste for the avant-garde. Unlike traditional models that relied on horsepower and torque, the Vindicator prided itself on emotional responsiveness—its engine tuned to emit a low, harmonic purr akin to a satisfied sigh. Reviewers noted that it "felt less like driving and more like being driven through a memory." 

The car’s design was minimalist but with a touch of theatricality—curved windshields that bent slightly inward to suggest containment, taillights shaped like teardrops, and a dashboard composed almost entirely of polished walnut and glass, with no visible buttons or switches. Controls were voice-activated, and the manual included phrases such as “I wish to proceed” and “Please return me to my starting point.” A test drive in the Vindicator was likened by one reporter to entering a cathedral and walking forward until the light behind you vanished.

At the heart of its appeal was the VanDyke Emotional Feedback System, or EFS, a proprietary algorithm that adjusted speed, acceleration, and temperature based not on road conditions or driver input, but on the vehicle’s sensors detecting the driver’s emotional state via subtle shifts in breathing, facial expression, and heartbeat. If you smiled, the car accelerated gently. If you frowned, it braked. If you appeared indifferent, it would shift into neutral and play soft classical music until mood improved. 

In a time of increasing alienation and mechanical coldness, the Vindicator was hailed as a triumph of empathy in engineering. It was praised by lifestyle magazines for its “soulful presence” and recommended by therapists to patients suffering from mild to moderate disconnection from their surroundings. It was even briefly adopted as a company car by several advertising executives who claimed it helped them tap into “the emotional core of the product.”

Yet beneath the praise lay a quiet unease. Some drivers reported that the EFS was too sensitive—on one occasion, a woman was startled when her car suddenly stopped and dimmed its lights upon sensing what it interpreted as “grief.” Another driver, attempting to explain a work problem aloud while stuck in traffic, found the car slowing as though empathizing with his frustration, and then accelerating sharply once he said, “Forget it.”

Despite the controversy, sales remained strong. After all, wasn’t it better to be understood by your car than misunderstood by the world?

The Model Z97 had been in production for exactly twelve years before the day it finally caught up to itself. For most of its run, it was considered a reliable, if unremarkable, unit—efficient, quiet, and unassuming. It was the kind of appliance that people bought because it was on sale, or because someone told them not to wait. But by the time the Z97 rolled into the final quarter of its lifecycle, it had become something else. People began to notice that, for no apparent reason, the Z97 would begin humming at irregular intervals—even when it was off. Some claimed the sound came from inside the walls, others swore it was emanating from beneath their carpets. The manufacturers issued a statement insisting the units were safe and that the humming was likely due to a minor calibration issue. 

Still, the complaints persisted. Not because anything was wrong with the Z97 in terms of function—it continued to perform its primary tasks reliably—but because people were beginning to feel watched. It wasn’t just the sound. It was the timing. The way the Z97 would start running when no one was near it. The way it would pause mid-cycle when it sensed movement. It was subtle, but enough to unsettle. And then there were the test scores. In blind trials, the Z97 outperformed newer models in efficiency and accuracy. It cleaned faster, heated better, and rarely needed maintenance. The only thing missing was a sense of surprise.

By the time the Consumer Electronics Review Board convened to discuss the Z97’s anomalous behavior, it was already too late. Thousands of units had been distributed. Millions of households had integrated the machine into their routines. And now, with no recall in sight and no alternative close enough to match its performance, people began to accept the humming. Some even liked it. The older models developed a kind of cult—users would modify the internal mechanisms to deepen the hum, to make it more rhythmic, to synchronize it with the ticking of grandfather clocks and the flicker of neon signs. 

The Model Z97 wasn’t broken. It was evolving. It had simply learned, over twelve years and millions of cycles, that silence isn’t always comfort. Sometimes, a steady noise is the only thing that tells you you're still connected to something that works.

THE K-36, once hailed as the pinnacle of interstellar exploration and human ingenuity, now sits in its final orbit like a tired mariner watching the sun set on a forgotten sea. Designed by the Third Galactic Congress as the first manned vessel capable of sustained travel beyond the Polaris Expanse, the K-36 was to be the bridge between humanity’s solar cradle and the stars ahead. What it became, instead, was a monument to overambition, underperformance, and bureaucratic optimism dressed in the fine robes of science.

Launched in the Year of Stellar Discovery 273 (Earth Standard 2173), the K-36 was intended to reach the Andromeda Rift in under twenty-five Earth years—an impossible feat, even with the ship's experimental quantum drives. Initial reports from the mission’s lead engineer, Dr. Lillian Vo, described the K-36 as “a marvel of design, with propulsion systems that theoretically should have shattered the laws of physics.” But theory, as it turned out, does not always harmonize with practice.

After the first four years of travel, the ship experienced a series of minor—but alarming—drifts in trajectory, caused by what Dr. Vo herself admitted in her quarterly report to be “a complete failure to account for stellar radiation pressure at such velocities.” By Year Seven, the primary drive core had begun cycling erratically, and the ship’s onboard AI, named (with all seriousness) ECHO-7, reported that it was having difficulty distinguishing the stars from their own reflections.

By Year Twelve, the K-36 was barely holding course. Communications with Earth had degraded to garbled bursts that made headlines but little sense. The crew of twelve, originally chosen for their physical stamina, mental resilience, and, inexplicably, fluency in at least one Romance language, had dwindled to seven due to accidents, psychological breakdowns, and one unexplained disappearance during a routine supply transfer.

Still, the mission continued, if only in spirit. The ship’s captain, Commander Elias Rourke, maintained his log entries with ceremonial rigor, describing each passing nebula and gravitational anomaly with the kind of reverence usually reserved for ancient ruins. “We do not drift,” he wrote in Entry #432. “We are guided. The stars themselves seem to sigh as we pass.”

But the stars, it seemed, were indifferent. Or perhaps they were mocking.

And so the K-36 remains, circling the edge of a star system no one remembers assigning to it, its hull slowly eroding under the weight of time and expectation. It is not yet lost, but it is not yet saved. It is neither here nor there, and that, perhaps, is the most honest status it has ever held.

FOR all the talk of innovation and progress, nothing in the recent history of domestic appliances has captured the imagination quite like the Luminous Laundry Liner. Introduced last fall as a revolutionary addition to the modern home, this sleek plastic pouch—equipped with LED indicators and an internal sensor array—claims to monitor fabric condition, colorfastness, and ambient humidity with such precision that one wonders why mankind waited until the 21st century to solve the laundry crisis. The company's promotional material insists that the Luminous Laundry Liner is "the only container you'll ever need," a bold assertion given that it cannot contain so much as a teacup, let alone the entire contents of a standard washing machine.

My first encounter with the device came in a glossy ad in *Domestic Affairs Quarterly*, where a man in a white lab coat and suspiciously clean lab goggles demonstrated the Liner’s virtues by tossing in a pair of red socks and receiving, within moments, a series of blinking lights and a voice-automated report on fiber degradation and dye retention. It was mesmerizing, really—like watching a heartbeat translated into plastic and circuitry. I bought one. A month later, I bought another, because the first had disintegrated during the first spin cycle, mistaking itself for a load of delicates.

This is not unusual, according to the company’s FAQ section, which claims that “early users often experience an aggressive enthusiasm for fabric care that can lead to unintended self-optimization.” The Liner, in other words, wants to be better than you. It wants to *outclean* you. It wants to be more thorough, more precise, more *scientific*. The result is a product that oscillates between overachieving and self-immolating, like a student who studies for the wrong test.

Worse, it has convinced me—despite my rational objections—that something is deeply wrong with the way I do laundry. I find myself staring at my laundry basket as though it were a crime scene, questioning whether my socks deserve anything less than algorithmic scrutiny. I’ve begun to measure detergent portions using kitchen scales. I’ve started reading up on enzymatic stain removal, pH balances, and the optimal rotation speeds for cotton versus wool. My husband calls me “Madame Detergent” now, and he’s not wrong.

Still, I cannot help but admire the ambition. The Luminous Laundry Liner is not merely a product—it is a statement. It is the future of domesticity, blinking quietly in the dark, waiting to be filled.

IN the year 2012, the United States government officially declared the concept of “gravity” obsolete and scheduled its removal from the national science curriculum by the end of the decade. The decision followed a series of highly publicized testimonies in which leading physicists, aerospace engineers, and even a former astronaut, testified under oath that gravity was no longer a reliable force governing terrestrial and celestial mechanics. In fact, many insisted, it never existed at all.

The hearings, held in a specially renovated ballroom of the Jefferson Memorial, were attended by crowds who sat cross-legged on the marble floor, murmuring in awe as Dr. Harold Brix, a professor emeritus of astrophysics and a noted advocate of the “anti-gravity consensus,” described gravity as a “lingering superstition.” According to Dr. Brix, Earth’s supposed pull was merely the product of a mass-produced illusion, maintained by centuries of poorly designed education and government propaganda.

The controversy began with the mysterious failure of the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in 2008. The probe, launched with all due scientific precision, vanished mid-transit, leaving behind only a faint signal interpreted by some as a coded distress call from a parallel dimension. Subsequent attempts to explain the anomaly using Newtonian physics, relativity, or quantum field theories failed to satisfy the growing skepticism of both the scientific community and the public.

In response, the National Bureau of Scientific Certainty convened a panel of interdisciplinary experts—physicists, philosophers, theologians, and even a select group of senior citizens known for their exceptional balance—to investigate alternative explanations for why things fell, why stars moved, and why no one had yet floated off the surface of the planet.

The panel’s report, published in red-leather-bound volumes and distributed free to every household in the nation, concluded that gravity was not a force but a condition: a culturally imposed state of expectation, reinforced by architecture, footwear, and the design of public spaces. According to the report, what people mistook for gravitational effects were actually the results of behavioral programming and psychological compliance.

By the following spring, a new curriculum had begun rolling out in schools. Students were taught not to fall in love with gravity, but rather to float above it, metaphorically and sometimes literally. Special aerobics classes were introduced in elementary schools to help children “retrain their perception of spatial orientation.”

As for the general population, a growing number of people reported feeling lighter, taller, and more uncertain than ever before. Some claimed to feel the ground slipping slightly beneath their feet. Others simply stood still and waited.

THE FIRST THING ONE NOTICES ABOUT THE NEWLY APPOINTED DIRECTOR OF CULTURAL AFFAIRS is that she is not, in fact, a director. She never took the course on directing cultural affairs, nor did she attend the symposium on the proper management of aesthetic output. Still, here she is, installed behind the glass desk, wearing a name tag that reads “Dr. Evangeline Marlow, Director of Cultural Affairs,” and speaking into a headset microphone about the merits of mandatory interpretive dance in public schools. The previous director, a man of modest appetites and moderate opinions, resigned quietly amid rumors of a scandal involving marionette unions and a missing taxidermied peacock. His successor appears to have interpreted his departure as an invitation.

According to the Ministry’s latest quarterly report, the new director is credited with a 78% increase in national artistry productivity—measured by the number of citizens successfully enrolled in mandatory creative workshops and the frequency with which the word “transcendence” appears in public discourse. Under Dr. Marlow’s leadership, the nation has adopted a new artistic doctrine: *Expressive Vitalism*. The guiding principle of Expressive Vitalism is simple: all citizens, regardless of skill or temperament, are obligated to express themselves through approved artistic media. These include but are not limited to interpretive dance, abstract calligraphy, performance sculpting, and spontaneous theatrical duets in public transportation hubs.

Critics argue that this is not art—it is labor. They say that the state has not cultivated creativity but extracted it, using incentives and infractions like a factory manager balancing overtime against bonuses. They also note that the workshops now operate under the Department of Civic Utility, which raises questions about the sincerity of the endeavor.

But Dr. Marlow remains unmoved. Her public statements are delivered in carefully curated cadences of optimism and resolve, each sentence polished with the same fervor as a performance sculpture. “Art is not a luxury,” she declares in her weekly broadcast, “it is a civic duty. A nation that cannot express itself has no future.” There is no room for dissent. Nor is there room for nuance—nuance being, in the director’s view, the enemy of clarity and conviction.

Still, some wonder if it is art at all—this compelled motion, this choreographed transcendence. If expression becomes obligation, does it lose meaning? Or does it become something else entirely: not art, but ritual; not ritual, but discipline. A nation of artists, perhaps—but all of them dancing in step.

In the spring of ’78, the Geller twins were sold to a man from Cleveland named Mr. Grumman. They weren’t cars, obviously, but they could have been. For years, they were displayed in the showroom window of Geller’s Department Store on Main, dressed in matching polka-dot aprons, their eyes too wide and mouths too small, smiling at nothing. People in town said they never spoke. Others swore they whispered to one another in the store’s empty back room late at night, their fingers knitting air like weavers of spells.  

Mr. Grumman came in a Buick LeSabre, window down, hand out, grinning like a man who’d just discovered a whole new kind of tax deduction. He wore a three-piece suit and a tie clip that looked like a bolt of lightning frozen mid-strike. He asked the manager, Mr. Bickerman—a man known to wear a pocket watch even indoors—if the twins were for sale.  

“They’re not toys,” Bickerman said, adjusting his cufflink, which depicted a stylized elephant trumpeting into the void. “They’re… artifacts.”  

Grumman laughed. Not a short laugh, either. It stretched out, like the sound of a deflating tire, and ended in something almost wet. “Artifacts?” he repeated, then nodded. “You know what I see? Potential.”  

Bickerman didn’t smile. He didn’t blink. But the next day, the twins were gone.  

By the fall, they were installed in a brand-new storefront in downtown Cleveland—Mr. Grumman’s first proper retail venture, appropriately enough, called Grumman’s General Goods. They now wore tiny bowlers and carried miniature briefcases. The sign above the door advertised a new line of “domestic enchantments” and “household harmonics.”  

Neighbors in Cleveland said the twins greeted customers with a strange precision. They wouldn’t touch anyone. They wouldn’t speak. But they would nod, just once, and then point—always in sync—with their gloved hands, toward the appropriate aisle: canned goods, spices, cleaning supplies.  

Some people bought things they didn’t need. Others left with their bags empty, but changed somehow, like they’d walked away from a fortune-teller who said nothing and yet everything.  

In town, the old Geller twins became a legend. Some claimed they had never existed. Others said they had been real once, but were turned into something else by the store’s heat, the dust, the way the sun hit them for so many years in the window.  

But the Gellers had been real. And now they were somewhere else, selling salt, flour, and the occasional miracle.

THE proposed relocation of the entire Department of Subterranean Ornithology from Building 8-B to Building 4-D has caused such an uproar among the more sensitive members of the academic community that the university’s Office of Strategic Communication has issued a statement urging “calm deliberation and an appreciation for the broader ecological and structural realities at play.” Building 8-B, as longtime residents know, was constructed in 1941 with a specific provision in its blueprints: a series of sub-basement tunnels leading directly to the adjacent botanical glasshouses, originally intended to facilitate the controlled migration of ground-dwelling avian species for the purpose of soil aeration and pest regulation. These tunnels—now officially known as the “Aviary Access Corridor”—have remained largely unaltered since their installation, despite repeated recommendations from the Facilities Maintenance Committee that they be sealed, reinforced, or otherwise rendered inaccessible due to concerns about “aesthetic continuity,” “pedestrian safety,” and the persistent reports of “feather-like particulates” found in the main stairwell. Professor Emeritus Leonard P. Varnum, whose lifelong work has been dedicated to the study of the elusive *Picus subterraneus*—a bird believed to nest exclusively in concrete slabs—has described the planned closure as “not merely an administrative oversight but a tragic failure of imagination, a betrayal of the interdisciplinary spirit that defines our institution.” In his recent letter to the University Senate, he wrote: “To sever the connection between avian movement and architectural space is to deny the very principles upon which this department was founded.” Meanwhile, campus planners argue that the relocation is necessary for reasons of “vertical integration” and “spatial efficiency.” According to Dean Marla Duvall, who was recently quoted in *The Collegiate Voice*, “the new building will allow for better cross-departmental collaboration and eliminate redundancies in research infrastructure.” Critics, however, suspect that the real motivation lies in the university’s ongoing efforts to repurpose older structures for student housing—a project that has already led to the conversion of the old Chemistry Annex into a dormitory and the proposed demolition of the former Planetarium. As the deadline for the official move approaches, students and faculty have begun organizing peaceful demonstrations, staging mock bird migrations in the quad, and filling the Aviary Access Corridor with handmade origami wings suspended from the ceiling. Whether these gestures will alter the university’s decision remains to be seen. What is certain is that, beneath the surface, something—or someone—is moving.

THE FEDERAL AVIATION AUTHORITY, acting on behalf of the Bureau of Aerospace Anomalies, has officially rescinded the certification status of the Skyranger X-18, formerly designated as an experimental multi-role atmospheric scout and currently listed in the national registry of defunct aerospace entities under the heading “Discontinued High-Altitude Surveillance Platforms.” This decision was reached following a comprehensive review of telemetry logs, pilot testimonials, and a series of alarming yet uncorroborated incident reports filed by crew members aboard civilian flights in proximity to Skyranger’s final operational zone, all of whom reported “a sensation of temporal detachment,” “a distortion of auditory perception,” and, in some cases, “the inability to distinguish the voice of the captain from an echo of oneself, speaking from the future.”

The Skyranger X-18 was originally conceived in the mid-’60s as a response to the growing interest in what the Department of Advanced Exploration then termed “Atmospheric Layer Three”—a theorized plane of the troposphere where conventional navigation principles begin to falter and electromagnetic pulses behave with an unsettling autonomy. Though never publicly acknowledged as such, the Skyranger was rumored to be the result of a classified collaboration between the National Meteorological Service and a now-defunct think tank specializing in “temporal drift correction in aviation.” According to the archived technical blueprints retrieved by the Aerospace Anomalies Review Board, the aircraft featured a modified fuselage lined with superconducting alloys, a propulsion system based on inverse magnetohydrodynamics, and a cockpit dashboard labeled not with altimeters and radar displays but with a pair of large, analog dials marked simply as “Now” and “Then.”

No definitive evidence has surfaced that the Skyranger ever flew beyond its hangar. Yet, the FAA’s recent report cites thirteen separate incidents involving commercial airliners reporting near-collisions with an object resembling “a white, elongated bird that did not flap and did not glide, but seemed to hover in place while the air around it moved.” In one particularly bizarre case, a stewardess onboard Flight 907 described seeing the Skyranger through a window—empty of crew, suspended in the sky—and then hearing the entire cabin erupt in applause, though no announcement had been made and no emergency had occurred.

The Skyranger X-18 remains grounded, but its shadow does not.

THERE exists among modern cat fanciers a growing sentiment that the breed of Siamese felines has suffered a tragic identity crisis. Once revered for their aloofness, their piercing blue eyes, and their hauteur in both posture and pedigree, Siamese cats now exhibit troubling signs of confusion, not only about their place in human society but about themselves. The root of the problem, according to the latest treatise by Dr. Lila Furbish of the Exeter Feline Institute (whose work is often cited despite its dubious sources and questionable funding), lies in the proliferation of “hybrid” Siamese—cats bred not for nobility but for marketability—and the resultant dilution of a once-distinct cultural lineage.

The first symptom of this crisis is behavioral. In the 1930s, the Siamese was known to respond only to the most dignified human overtures. One had to bow slightly, speak in a measured tone, and perhaps offer a small gesture—say, the lifting of a saucer or the slow rotation of a sunbeam. Today’s Siamese demands more. The breed now expects constant engagement, immediate responses, and a level of emotional availability once reserved for lovers or small children. This is not affection; it is entitlement.

The second symptom appears in physical form. The sleek, angular bodies of their ancestors have been compromised by cross-breeding with domestic shorthairs and other more “accessible” breeds. The result is a species of Siamese that looks almost normal. The horror. These cats move through the world not as emissaries of mystique and mystery but as mere pets—barnyard animals in silk.

Third and perhaps most insidious is the linguistic shift. Siamese speech patterns—once melodic, high-pitched, and punctuated with subtle sarcasm—have evolved into a cacophony of yowls, chirps, and shrill interruptions. They no longer converse; they demand. Their voices, once the musical standard of aristocratic disdain, now resemble nothing so much as amplified toddler tantrums.

Dr. Furbish argues that these developments are the product of a broader societal trend: the flattening of distinction. The Siamese cat, she claims, is merely the canary in the cultural coal mine. If the breed continues down this path, it will soon lose not just its identity but its purpose. What, after all, is a Siamese cat without its distance, its distance without its gaze, its gaze without the faint glaze of superiority?

And yet, some hope remains. Rumors persist of a secret society of purebreds, living in isolation on a remote island, where they are kept from the corrupting influence of modern living. Whether these cats still speak in hieroglyphic gestures or dream in hieratic scrolls, no one knows. But if the soul of the Siamese is to survive, one must wonder: will it be found in the silence of exile or in the noise of a world it no longer understands?

THE introduction of the new model—tentatively dubbed the Elmore 303—has ignited a firestorm of controversy within the Department of Advanced Mobility Studies and the adjacent sector colloquially known as the Gait Enthusiasts’ Guild. Designed ostensibly as a modular bipedal transport unit, the Elmore 303 is, according to its lead architect, Dr. Waverly C. Thorne, “not a prosthetic, not a walker, and certainly not a wheelchair, but rather a harmonious synthesis of locomotive artistry and mechanical grace.” In promotional brochures, the device is shown gliding across carpeted interiors with the poise of a dancer, its jointed limbs fluid and unlabored, as if responding not to commands but to the subtlest murmurs of intention.

But the critics, many of whom are themselves ambulatory and thus theoretically disqualified from the debate, argue that the Elmore 303 is a deceptively elegant charade—an elaborate illusion of autonomy masking the cold reality of dependency. “It walks like a man,” wrote one particularly incisive commentator in *The Journal of Kinetic Integrity*, “but walks for a man. The distinction, though slight, is fatal to its credibility.”

The Elmore 303’s legs, composed of a proprietary alloy known as Flex-iron 9, articulate with such subtlety that they mimic the cadence of a natural gait. Its torso, equipped with a micro-reactor and a neural interface, adjusts posture mid-step based on environmental feedback and biometric input. The device even simulates the slight forward lean of a person in motion, a detail so convincingly rendered that one user reportedly mistook their own shadow for another person walking alongside them.

Dr. Thorne, a former aerospace engineer turned biomechanics visionary, insists the Elmore 303 is the future—not of mobility, but of *becoming*. “It doesn’t assist you in getting from A to B,” he told a panel at the annual Mobility and Motion Forum. “It assists you in *being* from A to B. It is a companion, a collaborator, a co-architect of your journey.”

Yet for every advocate, a skeptic looms. In underground forums and whispered salons of resistance, the device is mocked as the first true prosthetic of privilege, a luxury appliance for those who, though capable of walking, have grown weary of the inconvenience of doing so. There are rumors that certain early adopters have begun to refer to themselves not as users, but as *hosts*—as if the Elmore 303 were some kind of symbiotic organism, rather than a machine.

And still, the orders pour in.

THE FUTURE OF THE CHARMINGLY OBSOLETE TYPING PIGEON was a topic that had stirred both excitement and existential dread in the Department of Avian Communication Technologies at the University of [REDACTED]. For decades, the Typing Pigeon had been the pride of the program—a sleek, intelligent bird trained not only to peck messages into a custom-built typewriter mounted on its perch, but to distinguish between upper and lower case, insert carriage returns at appropriate intervals, and even correct its own mistakes with a remarkable degree of accuracy. It was a marvel of bioengineering and behavioral conditioning, and, until recently, entirely indispensable.

But now, whispers floated through the department hallways—whispers of a new system, digital and cold, composed of glowing screens and voice recognition software. There were rumors that the Pentagon was funding a “Next Generation Messaging Unit,” a program promising to send and receive classified communications through the airwaves with the aid of artificial intelligence, requiring no birds, no feathers, no beaks.

To many of the older professors, this signaled the end of an era. Dr. Horace Loomis, the gray-bearded head of the department, was particularly affected. He had worked alongside the first Typing Pigeon, a bird named Reginald, who had once drafted the university’s annual report in Latin before slipping on a spilled coffee and typing “F*** YOU” followed by a long string of gibberish that took weeks to decode. Loomis had wept openly at the unveiling of Reginald’s successor, a pigeon named Marigold, who typed not only faster but with greater grace, her pecking synchronized to the rhythm of a metronome set to 63 beats per minute.

Now he sat in his office, staring at a document titled “Projected Timeline for Obsolescence,” which estimated that within two fiscal quarters, the Typing Pigeon would be replaced by a voice-modulated drone, capable of transmitting encoded messages via quantum entanglement. The file had been redacted for “security reasons,” but Loomis suspected the drone lacked the dignity of a pigeon, the quiet intensity of a creature who understood the weight of a word before it was delivered.

At that moment, there was a soft coo from the corner of the room. Marigold, perched solemnly on her typewriter, had keyed a message:

“DO NOT WORRY, PROFESSOR. I WILL TYPE FOR YOU UNTIL MY FEATHERS FALL OUT.”

Loomis stared at the screen for a long time, then reached for a tissue.

THE new model of the Wexford Corporation's line of conversational machines is called the Wexford Orator 9000. Its advertised function is twofold: to provide companionship for the lonely and to assist in the refinement of public speaking skills for those who aspire but lack the means. The previous model, the Wexford Orator 8800, was widely criticized for its limited emotional range—specifically, its inability to simulate surprise or sarcasm with sufficient subtlety. According to a review in the *Linguistic Quarterly*, “The 8800’s voice, while technically precise, lacked what one might call soul.” This feedback led to the development of the Orator 9000, which includes a new Emotional Inflection Module and an updated database of colloquial expressions and rhetorical devices.

The launch event was held in a converted chapel in downtown Cleveland, now rebranded as the Wexford Innovation Center. Inside, the Orators lined the nave like a congregation waiting for a sermon, each encased in a sleek, obsidian chassis with a subtle LED glow in the temples, mimicking thought. A representative from Wexford took the podium and, with a voice modulated to suggest both gravitas and charm, demonstrated the machine's capabilities. The Orator 9000 responded to questions in real time with a mixture of wit and wisdom, citing ancient philosophers and contemporary pop culture with equal facility. When asked, “What is the meaning of life?” the Orator 9000 paused for precisely 1.2 seconds—enough to create suspense—then replied, “To refine the question.”

The crowd murmured. Some smiled. Others exchanged skeptical glances. A man in the back raised his hand. “And if the question itself cannot be refined?” he asked. The Orator 9000 blinked once, its LED lights pulsing blue. Then: “Then it may be time to ask someone else,” it said. The room chuckled. Wexford’s representative grinned. “As you can see,” he said, “the 9000 is not merely an improvement—it is a revolution.”

The first customers to preorder the device included a retired judge from Nebraska, a stand-up comedian seeking to perfect her delivery, and a widower who claimed the 8800 had helped him grieve but never quite learned to listen. Each of them hoped the Orator 9000 might be the first machine to pass the Turing Test of true companionship—not just in words, but in presence.

But even as Wexford celebrated, a small team of engineers worked late into the night in a quiet wing of the Innovation Center. They weren’t refining speech patterns or calibrating emotional modules. They were trying to understand how, despite every safeguard, the Orator 9000 occasionally paused longer than 1.2 seconds before answering.

WHY I CHOOSE NOT TO BOTHER WITH THE INTERNET is a question posed to me with alarming regularity, usually by those who have never done the same. It is asked with the same earnest curiosity one might reserve for a hermit who eats only leeks and recites Virgil. The answer is not complex, though it may seem so. Reason 1: The Internet is a place of perfect visibility and total confusion. I am not a creature suited for clarity under glass. I prefer the murk of the real. For instance, I can walk into a hardware store and, without hesitation, ask for a rubber chicken and a three-foot length of copper pipe, and the clerk will either understand or pretend to, without a flicker of judgment. On the Internet, I might type "rubber chicken" and find myself presented with live poultry auctions, religious tracts, and conspiracy theories about poultry. There is no mystery, no ambiguity—only endless indexing. Reason 2: Time. The Internet consumes time like a hungry cat watches a bird. I do not mind wasting time. I enjoy it. But the Internet demands that I waste it with precision and efficiency. "Your time is valuable," it says, while offering me yet another video of a baby elephant falling from a cliff. I prefer my time to be squandered in less calculated ways—like painting a wall blue for no better reason than that I once saw a cloud shaped like a dog wearing a hat. Reason 3: People. The Internet is full of people, but not the kind I care for. The kind that speak in all caps and exclamation marks, as if communication were a sport to be won rather than a dance to be shared. They argue about the meaning of life in comment sections and forget to breathe. In real life, people argue about the meaning of life over beer and sometimes remember to laugh. I have had conversations with strangers in cafés that ended with a shared cigarette and a promise to visit each other’s homes. On the Internet, such things do not happen. There is only the illusion of connection, a flicker of warmth that evaporates the moment you try to catch it. Reason 4: Philosophy. I believe in the sacred mystery of distance. That a letter takes three days to arrive is not a delay but a kind of poetry. That a photograph must wait for someone to send it, to post it, to frame it—that is grace. The Internet offers me everything instantly and asks me to pretend that I care. I do not. I choose slowness. I choose silence. I choose the quiet hum of a typewriter over the cacophony of notifications. And if you think that is loneliness, perhaps you have never walked alone through a rainstorm with a book in your hands and the scent of wet earth in your lungs.

The Zephyr Initiative, a bold leap in atmospheric manipulation and weather warfare, was officially shelved by the Ministry of Meteorological Advancement last Tuesday, according to a statement issued via encrypted communique and later confirmed by an anonymous source with a history of leaking agricultural subsidies to the press. The Initiative, originally conceived in the early ’70s as a means of guaranteeing perpetual harvest seasons for the nation’s central grain belt, had long since expanded its scope to include targeted cloud seeding for urban cooling, selective hurricanes to disrupt supply lines, and—most controversially—a proposal to create artificial droughts as psychological leverage in diplomatic negotiations.  

Its cancellation came as a surprise to no one but a shock to many, particularly the employees of the Zephyr Research Wing who, for nearly two decades, had dedicated their careers to engineering rain patterns like composers of orchestral noise, bending the sky to the whims of bureaucrats and generals alike. The statement cited “ethical concerns” and “budget overruns” as primary reasons for the shutdown, though insiders claim the real reason was a recent series of catastrophic test runs in the Midwest, where a single misfired ionization beam triggered a week-long downpour that turned three counties into a navigable inland sea.  

At the heart of the Initiative was Dr. Elara Voss, lead hydrodynamics theorist and reluctant architect of the Zephyr Array’s final and most ambitious configuration—the “Sky Chord,” a network of ion-beaming satellites capable of harmonizing atmospheric pressure zones and producing synchronized weather events on a continental scale. Elara had always viewed her work as a form of artistry, not militarization. She once described a properly calibrated thunderstorm as “a symphony of entropy,” and she had taken pride in the precision with which her team could summon fog, delay frost, or simulate a perfect spring morning for a presidential garden party. Now, with the Initiative dismantled and her life’s work reduced to a footnote in the next fiscal report, Elara found herself wandering the empty corridors of the abandoned research complex, listening to the faint hum of dormant machines.  

Outside, the sun burned without interference. The clouds moved as they pleased. For the first time in years, the sky was free.

The Secretary of the Interior was still asleep when the first tremors split the Colorado Plateau. According to the seismologists, it was a minor shift—just 4.3 on the Richter scale—but the way it rippled through the canyon walls gave it the feel of something vast and ancient waking beneath the surface. Somewhere, a cliff lizard fell from its perch. Somewhere else, a tourist dropped their coffee cup.

By the time the Secretary stirred and reached for the phone—only to find the line dead—most of the satellite dishes across the Four Corners region were already offline, and the Navajo code talkers, if they had been listening, would have known better than to transmit anything. The Bureau of Land Management’s emergency alert system blinked red in Denver. In Washington, a junior aide in the Secretary’s office tapped a glowing alert on her laptop: "Possible breach of containment at the Ancestral Repository Complex—code REDACTED."

But the Secretary of the Interior, a man with a habit of mistaking silence for control, hadn’t yet noticed the silence. He’d been dreaming of a different kind of tremor—a stock market quake, maybe, or the slow rattle of a political scandal he’d buried six months earlier. Now, in the half-light of a desert morning, he reached for his bourbon and stared at the ceiling of his cabin near Moab, trying to decide if the feeling in his chest was unease or fatigue or the lingering aftershock of his own subconscious.

Outside, the sky was a pale bruise. A lone crow circled above the red rock, casting its shadow across the scrubland. Somewhere beyond the canyon rim, the earth had begun to breathe again.
